This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt presents Bridged Simulation-Based Inference (Bridged SBI) as a multi-fidelity Bayesian calibration approach for particle-based simulators, particularly DEM-like robotic earthwork and granular-soil systems. Direct high-fidelity (HF) SBI is computationally expensive because smaller particles and larger particle counts substantially increase simulation cost. Low-fidelity (LF) simulators use coarser, larger particles and fewer particles, making them cheaper, but changes in particle size and count alter collision frequency, energy dissipation, and other dynamics. Consequently, LF posteriors can be systematically biased relative to the HF posterior, with shifted parameter regions for friction, restitution, and related particle properties. Bridged SBI treats the LF posterior as an imperfect but informative guide rather than a direct HF approximation. It first uses inexpensive LF simulations to identify a coarse, high-density parameter region, then uses a limited number of local HF simulations to learn a residual LF–HF discrepancy bridge. The learned correction transports LF posterior samples toward HF-consistent regions. The method is designed to avoid posterior miscoverage associated with naive sequential multi-fidelity SBI, while reducing the HF simulation burden and retaining the likelihood-free, black-box nature of SBI. Reported experiments include sim-to-sim particle-parameter calibration and real-to-sim calibration with real soil observations, showing improved HF posterior accuracy and reliability under limited HF costs.

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table comparing model classes for small powder datasets (10-40 materials), including their suitability, advantages, and limitations. Include:

1. PLS/OPLS - Well suited (10-40 materials), implicit regularization via latent variables, handles collinear descriptors, ~20 materials for stable performance (Cao 2024), interpretable loadings, but linear

2. Ridge/Lasso - Suitable for small datasets, explicit L1/L2 regularization prevents overfitting, useful for variable selection (Lasso), linear, needs cross-validation for lambda

3. Gaussian Process Regression - Good for very small datasets, provides uncertainty estimates (posterior variance), kernel choice critical, can fail for non-smooth responses (GPR R²=0.384 for silo, but 0.976 for belt - Limhengha 2026)

4. Random Forest - Works with 30+ observations, handles nonlinearity, SHAP interpretable, robust, but may overfit with <30 samples, RF best for blend classification (~85% accuracy - Owasit 2025)

5. Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/CatBoost) - Needs more data than RF typically, good for regression, CatBoost used for FFc regression, GBM R²=0.883 for silo discharge (Limhengha 2026)

6. Neural Networks (MLP/DNN) - Risk of overfitting with <50 observations, but MLP best single-step classifier AUC-ROC=0.823 (Diaz 2023), DNN ensembles used in Abbas Digital Formulator, need regularization

7. Response Surface Methodology (RSM) - Excellent for small DoE (20-34 points), interpretable polynomial, R²=0.999 for belt angle (Limhengha 2026), but limited to low dimensionality

8. Bayesian latent-variable / multi-output models - Natural handling of uncertainty, useful for joint forward-inverse modeling, can incorporate priors from literature, limited published examples in feeding"}

### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Model class | Suitability for 10–40 materials | Main advantages | Main limitations / safeguards | Relevant evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS / OPLS | **Very suitable; recommended baseline.** Particularly useful when descriptors outnumber materials or are strongly correlated. | Latent variables provide implicit regularization; handles collinear flow, density and PSD descriptors; loadings/VIP scores aid interpretation; supports multi-response models. | Primarily linear; latent-component count must be selected inside cross-validation; interactions or transforms should be prespecified sparingly. In a 45-material study, reliability largely stabilized at about **20 representative materials**; stratified selection helped below 15. | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048) |
| Ridge / elastic net / lasso | **Suitable**, especially as a transparent benchmark with engineered physics features. | Explicit L2/L1 regularization controls variance; ridge is stable with correlated predictors; lasso can produce a compact descriptor panel; elastic net combines both benefits. | Linear unless interactions or splines are added; lasso may select one arbitrary member of a correlated group; scaling and nested selection of the penalty parameter are essential. | Ridge-regularized response surfaces were used successfully in a 34-point DEM-surrogate study (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000066). |
| Gaussian-process regression | **Excellent for very small, low-dimensional datasets** when calibrated uncertainty is important. | Posterior mean and variance support Bayesian calibration, active learning and constrained Bayesian optimization; kernels encode smoothness, monotonic trends and physics-informed distances. | Kernel and prior choices are decisive; sensitive to input scaling and non-smooth regime changes such as no-flow/flow transitions. With 34 DEM points, GPR achieved **R² = 0.976 ± 0.023** for belt mass flow but only **0.384** for nonlinear silo discharge. | (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000066) |
| Random forest | **Reasonable from roughly 30 independent observations**, or more when responses are highly variable. | Captures nonlinearities and interactions with little preprocessing; robust to monotone transforms; SHAP and permutation importance aid interpretation; useful for mixed continuous/categorical descriptors. | Piecewise-constant predictions extrapolate poorly; uncertainty is not inherently Bayesian; unstable feature importance under correlated predictors; can overfit tiny material-level datasets despite many within-material repeats. RF reached about **85%** two-class accuracy for constituent powders and **81.36%** on an unseen API. | (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000063) |
| Gradient boosting—XGBoost / CatBoost | **Potentially useful but usually more data-hungry than regularized linear models**; treat as a challenger rather than the primary model at 10–20 materials. | Strong nonlinear regression/classification; captures threshold effects and interactions; CatBoost handles categorical factors; SHAP interpretation is available. | Many hyperparameters create high selection variance; needs nested grouped validation, shallow trees and conservative regularization. GBM gave **R² = 0.883** for 34-point silo discharge, below ANN and RF; CatBoost has been used for FFc regression. | (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000063) |
| Neural networks—MLP / DNN | **Generally high risk below 40–50 independent materials** unless the architecture is tiny, strongly regularized or pretrained on simulation/library data. | Flexible multi-output mapping; can fuse distributions, images and scalar properties; ensembles provide empirical uncertainty; suitable for large simulation-generated datasets. | Parameter count can dwarf material count; repeated runs from the same material do not solve this; requires early stopping, weight decay, ensembling and material-grouped validation. MLP achieved **ROC-AUC = 0.823** on 112 powder systems; the Digital Formulator used 20-member DNN ensembles and leave-API-out testing. | (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036) |
| Response-surface methodology | **Excellent for designed simulation/experimental campaigns of about 20–34 points with few factors.** | Interpretable linear, quadratic and interaction terms; efficient for calibration and optimization; coefficients and derivatives expose physical trends. | Scales poorly with dimension; fixed polynomials miss discontinuities, hysteresis and complex local structure; design space must be bounded. With 34 DEM points, RSM achieved **R² = 0.999 ± 0.001** for belt discharge angle; a 20-run auger DEM design produced mean deviation **0.87%**. | (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000066) |
| Bayesian latent-variable / hierarchical multi-output models | **Conceptually best for the proposed 13–40-material campaign**, although implementation is more demanding and direct feeder precedents are limited. | Represents latent powder state, repeated-run variation, label uncertainty and correlated outputs jointly; incorporates literature values as uncertain priors; enables coherent forward prediction and Bayesian inversion; posterior uncertainty can drive active learning or BO. | Requires explicit identifiability constraints and careful priors; computation and diagnostics are more involved; posterior multimodality is likely when several DEM parameters produce similar fingerprints. Surrogates or multi-fidelity SBI may be needed for expensive DEM. | Bayesian DEM calibration supports parameter distributions and correlations; Bridged SBI reduced posterior KL divergence by up to **75%** versus naïve multi-fidelity inference under a small high-fidelity budget (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058). |


*Table: Comparison of model families for datasets containing roughly 10–40 independent powders, emphasizing data efficiency, uncertainty, nonlinear capability, and safeguards against material-level leakage.*

{"answer": "## Predicting Powder Dosing and Flow from Material Properties: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Published Forward and Inverse Models Linking Material Properties to Feeder/Doser Performance

The table below summarizes the principal studies identified that either predict feeder or doser performance from raw-material properties (forward models) or predict powder properties from process or flow signals (inverse models).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Forward models (properties → feeder performance).** The most systematic forward-model program is from the Ghent/FDA collaborative group. Bostijn et al. (2019) characterized 15 pharmaceutical powders with 25 descriptors spanning particle-size distribution, flow function (ffc), Hausner ratio, basic flow energy, compressibility, aeration response, and charge density, then built four separate PLS regressions predicting maximum feed factor (FFmax), feed-factor decay, feed-rate relative standard deviation (RSD), and relative error (RE) on a K-Tron MT12 twin-screw feeder; volumetric responses (FFmax, FFdecay) were predicted more successfully than gravimetric variability, while RE was only weakly related to material properties because values clustered near zero (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). Li (2020), extending the Rutgers/FDA framework of Wang et al. (2017), used 30 flow properties from 7–14 materials as inputs to PLSR models predicting refill disturbances (maximum deviation, deviation time, excess mass) on loss-in-weight feeders, validating with leave-one-material-out cross-validation and finding qualitatively successful prediction (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000010). Conditioned bulk density (cBD) emerged as the single strongest correlate of feed factor in that library, enabling approximate feeder and screw selection once cBD is known (pqac-00000010). Wang et al. **Surrogate model selection for DEM outputs.** Limhengha and Sudsawat (2026) compared five surrogate families—RSM, ANN, RF, GBM, and GPR—on 34 DEM design points for silo discharge and belt-conveyor responses. They found that the best algorithm is response-specific: ANN achieved R² = 0.964 for silo discharge mass flow rate, while GPR attained R² = 0.976 for belt mass-flow but only 0.384 for silo discharge, and RSM reached R² = 0.999 for belt discharge angle (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063). SHAP analysis confirmed physical expectations (outlet width dominated silo flow with 78.6% importance) and the proposed SHAP Asymmetry Ratio offered a diagnostic for algorithm pre-selection (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000064).

**Physics-informed features.** While granular Bond number (ratio of cohesive to gravitational force) and orifice-to-particle size ratio are well-established dimensionless groups in the powder-flow literature (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015), and Girnth et al. (2024) specifically advocated formula-based dimensionless DEM parameterization for additive manufacturing, the retrieved studies did not demonstrate a completed workflow using these features as explicit ML inputs for feeder prediction. Incorporating such physics-informed features into the user's PLS or GP models—for example, using the ratio of auger outlet diameter to D50 rather than each separately—would reduce dimensionality and improve out-of-domain extrapolation.

---

### 4. Dataset Size Requirements and Most Predictive Descriptors

**How many materials are needed.** For PLS models, Cao et al. (2024) found that 20 materials produced stable performance equivalent to 45 materials, and that hierarchical sampling gave more reliable few-shot models when libraries contained fewer than 15 materials (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047). For ML classifiers, Owasit et al. (2025) used 89 single-component measurements from 27 distinct materials to train RF classifiers achieving 85% accuracy (pqac-00000028). Bostijn et al. (2019) built useful PLS models from 13 calibration materials plus 2 external (pqac-00000004). Collectively, these suggest that 15–20 diverse materials provide a practical lower bound for regression models, while 10–13 may suffice for coarser classification or ranking tasks. The user's 13 powders, spanning more than three decades of mass per revolution, provide substantial diversity but are near the minimum; adding 7–12 materials (metal AM powders, sieved fractions, humidity-conditioned salt) as planned would substantially improve reliability.

**Most predictive descriptors for small feeders.** Across the literature, conditioned bulk density (cBD) emerges as the single strongest correlate of feed factor and mass flow rate in screw feeders (pqac-00000010). Beyond this, the most informative descriptor sets include: (i) compressibility at a defined stress, which reflects interparticle cohesion and predicts feed-factor decay at changing hopper levels (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015); (ii) flow-function coefficient (ffc) from shear-cell testing, the standard cohesion/flowability classifier (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000024); (iii) particle-size distribution measures D10, D50, and D90, with D10 and D50 identified as the most important SHAP features for FFc prediction (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030); (iv) particle shape (aspect ratio and sphericity), which affects mechanical interlocking and flow through small orifices (pqac-00000029); (v) permeability, which governs air-entrainment and de-aeration behavior during feeding (pqac-00000012); (vi) dynamic flow energy (BFE, specific energy, stability index), which reflects flow behavior under active agitation such as screw rotation (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008); and (vii) charge density, which was included in the Bostijn et al. descriptor set (pqac-00000004). Wall friction angle is important for hopper and die-filling contexts (pqac-00000024) but was not identified as a dominant feed-factor predictor. Moisture was recognized as influential through capillary forces and electrostatic effects (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015), though its role was not isolated in the retrieved feeder-specific models.

Wang et al. (2019) demonstrated that for routine flow characterization, a reduced set of four tests—compressibility, permeability, and shear-cell measurements at 3 and 9 kPa—captured flow-classification structure equivalent to the full test battery, consuming approximately 50 g and three instrument-hours per material (pqac-00000011). This represents a practical minimum measurement set for the user's planned characterization.

**Relevance to additive manufacturing spreadability.** Hall flow time does not correlate with spread-layer density in AM (pqac-00000043), consistent with the user's observation that Hausner ratio and d50 do not correlate with auger mass per revolution. The angle of repose, which did correlate with the user's dosing data (Spearman −0.84 at 45° tilt), is used in DEM calibration as a standard bulk-flow target (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) and is one of the most accessible single descriptors of interparticle friction, though it conflates friction and cohesion effects (pqac-00000019).

---

### 5. Forward–Inverse Model Consistency and Bayesian Optimization for New Materials

**Three architectures for consistency.** The user asks how a model predicting powder properties from dosing data (inverse) and a model predicting dosing from properties (forward) can be kept consistent. The literature suggests three approaches in order of increasing rigor:

(a) **Two separate regressions** is the simplest and most common approach in practice—one PLS or RF model maps properties to feed factor, another maps dosing behavior to a flowability class. This is how most pharmaceutical studies operate (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000029). The drawback is that the two models can be mutually inconsistent: a material classified as "cohesive" by the inverse model may be predicted to have acceptable feed factor by the forward model.

(b) **Bayesian inversion of a forward model** is the natural architecture for the user's DEM twin. The forward model (DEM or a trained surrogate) maps particle-level properties (friction, cohesion, rolling friction) to observable dosing fingerprints (mass per revolution, tap-freed mass, afterflow). Bayesian inference—using MCMC, sequential Monte Carlo, or simulation-based inference—then inverts the forward model to obtain a posterior distribution over particle properties given observed data. El Kassem et al. (2021) accomplished this via contour-plot intersection from a regression surrogate (pqac-00000020). Kim et al. (2026) demonstrated Bridged SBI for the same task, using neural posterior estimation with a residual correction bridge between low- and high-fidelity DEM (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000054). Fransen et al. (2025) reviewed Bayesian inference for granular-material simulations, formulating the state–parameter model with process and measurement uncertainties and noting that surrogate models (Gaussian processes, neural networks) are needed to make posterior sampling tractable (pqac-00000058). This architecture ensures automatic consistency: every property value that the inverse model returns is also the input that the forward model would use to predict the observed behavior.

(c) **A joint latent-variable model** would posit that each powder has a low-dimensional latent representation (e.g., a "flow phenotype") from which both the dosing fingerprint and the standard-test properties are generated. PCA or PLS already implicitly provide such a latent space when applied jointly to dosing and property data. No published study was found that implements a fully Bayesian joint latent-variable model specifically for powder dosing, though the pharmaceutical material-library framework of Wang et al. (2019) uses PCA to place materials in a latent space that simultaneously represents flow behavior, feeder performance, and material similarity (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014).

**Bayesian optimization for feeding/dosing of new materials.** The most advanced published implementation is the Digital Formulator and self-driving Tableting DataFactory of Abbas et al. (2025, 2026). The Digital Formulator uses a forward model—ensembles of 20 deep neural networks predicting tablet porosity and tensile strength from raw-material attributes, formulation composition, and compression pressure—validated by leave-API-out testing. It optimizes formulation to maximize flowability (ffc) while constraining tablet quality, using NSGA-II for in-silico search. The Tableting DataFactory then applies physics-informed Bayesian optimization to refine process parameters, typically converging in fewer than six iterations (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038). The powder-dosing system uses a volumetric dispenser whose chamber volume, vacuum duration, and air pressure are adjusted based on density and particle properties, with real-time weighing to reject doses outside ±5% of target (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). This platform demonstrates the principle of using a forward model to initialize process settings for a new material and then refining them via closed-loop Bayesian optimization—directly applicable to the user's auger doser.

For the user's system specifically, the recommended workflow would be: (1) measure a compact property set (angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, PSD by sieving or laser diffraction, and moisture) on each of the 13+ powders; (2) build a forward PLS or Gaussian-process model mapping these properties to the dosing fingerprint; (3) for Bayesian inversion, train a surrogate on the existing DEM twin (20–50 parameter combinations, each requiring 26–30 CPU-minutes), then use simulation-based inference or MCMC to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling-friction parameters given the observed fingerprint; (4) validate inferred values against measured properties where available; and (5) for a new powder, use the forward model's prediction as the initial setting and prior for Bayesian optimization of auger speed and tilt, closing the loop with the balance feedback already implemented. Multi-fidelity inference via Bridged SBI (pqac-00000051) could reduce the DEM budget by using coarse-grained simulations for initial exploration and full-resolution runs only for refinement."}

state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Our data so far: 13 powders (NaCl, Si 75-150 um and Si <44 um, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, Na2SO4, BaCl2 dihydrate, calcium lactate, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, sodium alginate, white and brown rice flour, fumed silica), each run once through a fixed protocol on a cone-exit auger: mass per revolution at 0, 22.5 and 45 degree tube tilt (30 rpm, six single revolutions each), a speed exponent from 15 to 90 rpm, mass released per solenoid tap, mass that flows during a 15 s static hold, and closed-loop doses of 50, 200 and 1000 mg (error, time, pass rate). Mass per revolution spans more than three decades and five powders barely convey. The property values we have are handbook or supplier values for each material class (angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, Hausner ratio, d50, true density, equilibrium moisture), not measurements on our lots, and their published ranges are wide (angle of repose ranges 6-16 degrees). Literature angle of repose correlates with log mass per revolution at 45 degrees (Spearman -0.84); d50 and Hausner ratio do not. We plan to measure angle of repose, PSD, bulk and tapped density and moisture on the same jars, to add powders (metal AM powders, sieved size fractions, humidity-conditioned salt), and we have the DEM twin described above. Questions: (1) Which published studies built statistical or machine-learning models that predict feeder or doser performance (feed factor, mass flow rate, flow variability, feeding capacity, refill behaviour, dosing accuracy) from raw-material properties, for example material property libraries with PCA or PLS for loss-in-weight, screw and micro-feeders, and which studies predicted powder properties (flowability class, ffc, Hausner ratio, cohesion, particle size, moisture) from process or flow signals (feeder, rotating drum or avalanche tester, vibrating capillary, hopper or funnel discharge)? For each, give the number of materials, the descriptors and responses, the model, the validation scheme and the accuracy reached. (2) For datasets of 10-40 materials, which model classes and practices work best (PLS, ridge or lasso, Gaussian processes, random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks, Bayesian latent-variable or multi-output models, monotone or physics-constrained models)? How should repeated measurements per material, censored responses (no flow), and noisy or literature-derived property labels be handled, and how should models be validated (leave-one-material-out, nested cross-validation, prospective tests on new materials)? (3) How have physics-based models (DEM, Beverloo, Jenike or screw-conveyor models) been combined with data-driven models in this setting: simulation-generated training data, physics-informed features such as granular Bond number or orifice-to-particle size ratio, residual or discrepancy learning, multi-fidelity or transfer learning, and with what measured gains? (4) How many materials and which measurements are typically needed to reach useful accuracy, and which descriptors have proven most predictive of flow in small feeders (cohesion or ffc, wall friction, bulk density, PSD width, particle shape, moisture, electrostatics)? (5) How can a model that predicts properties from dosing data and a model that predicts dosing from properties be kept consistent (one joint latent-variable model, Bayesian inversion of a forward model, or two separate regressions), and have such models been used to choose initial settings, priors or task descriptors for Bayesian optimization of feeding or dosing for a new material?

## Predicting Powder Dosing and Flow from Material Properties: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Published Forward and Inverse Models Linking Material Properties to Feeder/Doser Performance

The table below summarizes the principal studies identified that either predict feeder or doser performance from raw-material properties (forward models) or predict powder properties from process or flow signals (inverse models).

| Reference | Direction | Materials / datasets | Descriptors (X) | Responses (Y) | Model | Validation scheme | Reported accuracy |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bostijn et al. (2019) | Forward: properties → feeder performance | 15 pharmaceutical powders; 13 calibration + 2 external | 25 descriptors, including \(d_{v50}\), FFc, Hausner ratio, Carr index, BFE/nBFE, FRI, specific energy, compressibility, aeration response, and charge density; plus screw speed or feed-rate setpoint | Maximum feed factor (FFmax), feed-factor decay (FFdecay), feed-rate RSD, relative error (RE) | Separate PLS regressions | Leave-one-out CV for latent-variable selection; S1500 and API 3 as external powders | FFmax and FFdecay predicted better than gravimetric RSD and RE; RE was weakly related to properties; exact external-error values unavailable in retrieved text (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 18-22, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 10-14) |
| Li (2020), extending Wang et al. feeder framework | Forward: properties → refill behaviour | 7 powders in refill model; broader feeder study used 14 materials | 30 bulk/flow properties plus drive command needed to maintain 8 kg/h | Maximum refill deviation, deviation duration, and excess-mass fraction (%Total) | PLSR; PCA with weighted similarity scoring for qualitative material matching | Leave-one-material-out calibration; each powder treated as the unknown in turn | Predicted and measured refill deviations differed only slightly; no numerical R²/RMSE reported in retrieved text (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 78-82, li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 36-40) |

**Forward models (properties → feeder performance).** The most systematic forward-model program is from the Ghent/FDA collaborative group. Bostijn et al. (2019) characterized 15 pharmaceutical powders with 25 descriptors spanning particle-size distribution, flow function (ffc), Hausner ratio, basic flow energy, compressibility, aeration response, and charge density, then built four separate PLS regressions predicting maximum feed factor (FFmax), feed-factor decay, feed-rate relative standard deviation (RSD), and relative error (RE) on a K-Tron MT12 twin-screw feeder; volumetric responses (FFmax, FFdecay) were predicted more successfully than gravimetric variability, while RE was only weakly related to material properties because values clustered near zero (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 18-22, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6). Li (2020), extending the Rutgers/FDA framework of Wang et al. (2017), used 30 flow properties from 7–14 materials as inputs to PLSR models predicting refill disturbances (maximum deviation, deviation time, excess mass) on loss-in-weight feeders, validating with leave-one-material-out cross-validation and finding qualitatively successful prediction (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 78-82, li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 36-40). Conditioned bulk density (cBD) emerged as the single strongest correlate of feed factor in that library, enabling approximate feeder and screw selection once cBD is known (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 36-40). Wang et al. (2019) built a material library of approximately 20 powders with 30+ flow descriptors reduced via PCA; a reduced set of four tests—compressibility, permeability, and shear-cell measurements at two stresses—produced clustering equivalent to the full set, using about 50 g and three instrument-hours per material (wang2019developmentandapplications pages 19-23, wang2019developmentandapplications pages 10-15). Benedetti built a multivariate weighted PLS (MwPLS) model for a single material across 34 batches, predicting feed-factor profiles from hopper weight and flow-rate setpoint with calibration R² = 0.91 and external-validation R² averaging 0.87 (benedettiUnknownyeardataanalyticsfor pages 80-86). Rezaeizadeh (2026) compared PLS, random forest, Gaussian-process regression, and SVR for feed-factor-profile prediction, finding all models achieved MAPE < 5%, with PLS including material properties yielding RMSECV of 0.118 g versus 0.122 g for RF without material properties—a marginal improvement (rezaeizadeh2026applicationofmachine pages 48-50).

**Inverse models (process signals → powder properties).** Diaz et al. (2023) used 112 pharmaceutical systems (30 APIs, 43 excipients, 40 blends) characterized by dynamic image analysis (D10, D50, D90, aspect ratio, sphericity) and bulk density to classify powders into flow-function-coefficient (FFc) classes (cohesive, easy-flowing, free-flowing). Among six classifiers (MLP, RF, SVM, kNN, naïve Bayes, AdaBoost), MLP achieved the highest single-step ROC-AUC of 0.823 under 10-fold cross-validation, though the middle "easy-flowing" class was classified below 45% correct (diaz2023machinelearningmodels pages 97-102, diaz2023machinelearningapproaches pages 4-5, diaz2023machinelearningapproaches pages 3-4). In the companion thesis, a random-forest model on 103 formulations predicted continuous FFc with MAPE = 0.173 and wall-friction angle with MAE = 1.83°, using SHAP to reveal that API D10, D50, and aspect ratio D10 were the most predictive features (diaz2023machinelearningmodels pages 167-170). Owasit et al. (2025) assembled 410 blends from 9 APIs and 18 excipients, classifying flow regimes (2–5 classes defined by FFc thresholds) with RF, XGBoost, SVM, logistic regression, kNN, and MLP. RF performed best, reaching approximately 85% accuracy for two-class individual components, 94.67% for uncoated blends, and 81.36% on an entirely unseen API (IBU25) for two classes, though accuracy declined to 45.76% for five classes (owasit2025predictingpowderblend pages 17-18, owasit2025predictingpowderblend pages 1-2). SHAP analysis identified dry-coating parameters as the most influential features, followed by particle size and morphology (owasit2025predictingpowderblend pages 1-2).

---

### 2. Model Classes and Practices for Datasets of 10–40 Materials

The following table compares model families evaluated on small powder datasets.

|---|---|---|---|---|

*Table: Comparison of model families for datasets containing roughly 10–40 independent powders, emphasizing data efficiency, uncertainty, nonlinear capability, and safeguards against material-level leakage.*

**PLS as the recommended baseline.** For pharmaceutical material-library modeling, Cao et al. (2024) systematically investigated PLS sample-size requirements using a 45-material library with 27 physical-property descriptors predicting tablet tensile strength. Performance (minimum R² and RMSE) stabilized and remained nearly unchanged as sample size increased from 20 to 45 materials, indicating that approximately 20 diverse materials suffice for dependable PLS prediction (cao2024samplesizerequirements pages 1-2). Below 15 materials, hierarchical sampling based on a tabletability classification index d was more reliable than random sampling, reducing the incidence of low-quality few-shot models (cao2024samplesizerequirements pages 13-14). For the user's 13-material set, PLS is therefore feasible but near the lower limit; expanding to 20–25 materials with deliberately diverse flow behavior would improve stability.

**Handling repeated measurements, censored data, and noisy labels.** Multiple measurements per material (e.g., six single-revolution mass values at each tilt angle) should be treated as repeated measures within a material-level statistical unit, not as independent observations. Material should be the blocking factor in cross-validation (leave-one-material-out or grouped k-fold), as demonstrated by Wang/Li's leave-one-material-out scheme (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 78-82) and Limhengha et al.'s replicate-aware grouped five-fold cross-validation, which assigns all replicates of a design point to the same fold to prevent leakage (limhengha2026explainablesurrogatebasedknowledge pages 12-13). Censored responses (five powders that barely convey, yielding near-zero mass per revolution) can be handled by Tobit-style censored regression within PLS or by treating the threshold between "no flow" and "flow" as a binary classification layer preceding a continuous regression for flowing materials (a two-step scheme analogous to Diaz et al.'s two-step FFc classifier) (diaz2023machinelearningmodels pages 97-102). Literature-derived property values with wide reported ranges (e.g., angle of repose 6–16°) introduce label noise that can be modeled by Bayesian measurement-error or errors-in-variables extensions, or by treating literature values as informative priors and updating them as measured values become available (fransen2026towardsscientificmachine pages 14-16).

**Validation.** Leave-one-material-out cross-validation is the gold standard for material-level generalization with 10–20 materials (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 78-82). With more materials, nested cross-validation (inner loop for hyperparameter tuning, outer for performance estimation) is preferred. Prospective tests on genuinely new materials provide the strongest evidence: Bostijn et al. validated on two held-out powders (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 18-22), and Owasit et al. tested on an entirely unseen API (owasit2025predictingpowderblend pages 17-18).

---

### 3. Combining Physics-Based and Data-Driven Models

Several strategies for integrating DEM, Beverloo, Jenike, or screw-conveyor models with data-driven approaches have been demonstrated.

**DEM-generated training data.** Desai and Higgs (2019) calibrated a polydispersed DEM model of Ti-6Al-4V powder spreading against rheometer data, then ran approximately 50 virtual spreading simulations varying spreader translation and rotation speeds. The DEM outputs (retained mass, throughput, roughness, porosity) served as noise-free training data for a back-propagation neural network with one hidden layer of 200 sigmoid neurons. The trained surrogate achieved ≥96% accuracy and was used to generate spreading process maps, enabling rapid exploration that would be prohibitively expensive with DEM alone (desai2019spreadingprocessmaps pages 3-5, desai2019spreadingprocessmaps pages 12-14, desai2019spreadingprocessmaps pages 5-8). This approach maps directly onto the user's situation: each auger revolution costs 26–30 CPU-minutes in DEM, so a design of 20–50 DEM simulations spanning friction coefficients and speed could train a surrogate that runs in milliseconds.

**DEM-based calibration with DoE and regression.** El Kassem et al. (2021) used a vertical auger doser as the calibration device, extracting angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate as three experimentally measurable bulk responses. A D-optimal design of experiments varying four DEM input factors (auger speed, particle–particle static and rolling friction, particle–wall static friction) was simulated in LIGGGHTS with Hertz–Mindlin contact and EPSD2 rolling resistance. Multivariate regression analysis built prediction models from only 20 DEM simulations. Superimposing contour plots of the three predicted responses dramatically reduced admissible parameter combinations, yielding an optimized set with maximum deviation of 2.86% for dosing time and mean deviation of 0.87% across 12 bulk responses (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 1-2, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 5-6, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13). This workflow directly parallels the user's DEM twin and shows that multiple bulk responses (their dosing fingerprint) can be used jointly to constrain DEM parameters.

**Multi-fidelity and transfer learning.** Kim et al. (2026) introduced Bridged Simulation-Based Inference (Bridged SBI) for cost-efficient Bayesian calibration of particle-based simulators. The method uses inexpensive low-fidelity DEM simulations (coarser particles, fewer particles) to identify a coarse posterior region, then trains a residual correction or transport bridge using a small number of high-fidelity simulations. In real-to-sim experiments calibrating friction and restitution of granular soil from depth images, Bridged SBI achieved KL divergence of 2.79 ± 0.77 at a total budget of N = 7 high-fidelity evaluations, compared with 11.19 ± 6.80 for naïve multi-fidelity SBI and 6.53 ± 3.62 for high-fidelity-only SBI—a 75% and 67% reduction respectively (kim2026bridgedsbicorrecting pages 1-2, kim2026bridgedsbicorrecting pages 6-7, kim2026bridgedsbicorrecting pages 5-6). This approach is directly applicable to the user's scenario: a coarse-grained DEM at 6× particle diameter (as used by Kassem et al.) could serve as the low-fidelity simulator, while the current full-resolution model provides the high-fidelity simulator, with a small number of full-resolution runs used to debias the coarse posterior.

**Surrogate model selection for DEM outputs.** Limhengha and Sudsawat (2026) compared five surrogate families—RSM, ANN, RF, GBM, and GPR—on 34 DEM design points for silo discharge and belt-conveyor responses. They found that the best algorithm is response-specific: ANN achieved R² = 0.964 for silo discharge mass flow rate, while GPR attained R² = 0.976 for belt mass-flow but only 0.384 for silo discharge, and RSM reached R² = 0.999 for belt discharge angle (limhengha2026explainablesurrogatebasedknowledge pages 28-30, limhengha2026explainablesurrogatebasedknowledge pages 13-15). SHAP analysis confirmed physical expectations (outlet width dominated silo flow with 78.6% importance) and the proposed SHAP Asymmetry Ratio offered a diagnostic for algorithm pre-selection (limhengha2026explainablesurrogatebasedknowledge pages 2-4, limhengha2026explainablesurrogatebasedknowledge pages 23-25).

**Physics-informed features.** While granular Bond number (ratio of cohesive to gravitational force) and orifice-to-particle size ratio are well-established dimensionless groups in the powder-flow literature (wang2019developmentandapplications pages 15-19, li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 21-25), and Girnth et al. (2024) specifically advocated formula-based dimensionless DEM parameterization for additive manufacturing, the retrieved studies did not demonstrate a completed workflow using these features as explicit ML inputs for feeder prediction. Incorporating such physics-informed features into the user's PLS or GP models—for example, using the ratio of auger outlet diameter to D50 rather than each separately—would reduce dimensionality and improve out-of-domain extrapolation.

---

### 4. Dataset Size Requirements and Most Predictive Descriptors

**How many materials are needed.** For PLS models, Cao et al. (2024) found that 20 materials produced stable performance equivalent to 45 materials, and that hierarchical sampling gave more reliable few-shot models when libraries contained fewer than 15 materials (cao2024samplesizerequirements pages 13-14, cao2024samplesizerequirements pages 1-2). For ML classifiers, Owasit et al. (2025) used 89 single-component measurements from 27 distinct materials to train RF classifiers achieving 85% accuracy (owasit2025predictingpowderblend pages 1-2). Bostijn et al. (2019) built useful PLS models from 13 calibration materials plus 2 external (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 18-22). Collectively, these suggest that 15–20 diverse materials provide a practical lower bound for regression models, while 10–13 may suffice for coarser classification or ranking tasks. The user's 13 powders, spanning more than three decades of mass per revolution, provide substantial diversity but are near the minimum; adding 7–12 materials (metal AM powders, sieved fractions, humidity-conditioned salt) as planned would substantially improve reliability.

**Most predictive descriptors for small feeders.** Across the literature, conditioned bulk density (cBD) emerges as the single strongest correlate of feed factor and mass flow rate in screw feeders (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 36-40). Beyond this, the most informative descriptor sets include: (i) compressibility at a defined stress, which reflects interparticle cohesion and predicts feed-factor decay at changing hopper levels (wang2019developmentandapplications pages 15-19, li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 21-25); (ii) flow-function coefficient (ffc) from shear-cell testing, the standard cohesion/flowability classifier (wang2019developmentandapplications pages 15-19, diaz2023machinelearningmodels pages 167-170); (iii) particle-size distribution measures D10, D50, and D90, with D10 and D50 identified as the most important SHAP features for FFc prediction (diaz2023machinelearningapproaches pages 4-5, diaz2023machinelearningapproaches pages 1-2); (iv) particle shape (aspect ratio and sphericity), which affects mechanical interlocking and flow through small orifices (diaz2023machinelearningapproaches pages 4-5); (v) permeability, which governs air-entrainment and de-aeration behavior during feeding (wang2019developmentandapplications pages 15-19); (vi) dynamic flow energy (BFE, specific energy, stability index), which reflects flow behavior under active agitation such as screw rotation (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 18-22, wang2016usingmultivariateanalysis pages 68-73); and (vii) charge density, which was included in the Bostijn et al. descriptor set (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 18-22). Wall friction angle is important for hopper and die-filling contexts (diaz2023machinelearningmodels pages 167-170) but was not identified as a dominant feed-factor predictor. Moisture was recognized as influential through capillary forces and electrostatic effects (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 160-162, li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 21-25), though its role was not isolated in the retrieved feeder-specific models.

Wang et al. (2019) demonstrated that for routine flow characterization, a reduced set of four tests—compressibility, permeability, and shear-cell measurements at 3 and 9 kPa—captured flow-classification structure equivalent to the full test battery, consuming approximately 50 g and three instrument-hours per material (wang2019developmentandapplications pages 19-23). This represents a practical minimum measurement set for the user's planned characterization.

**Relevance to additive manufacturing spreadability.** Hall flow time does not correlate with spread-layer density in AM (desai2019spreadingprocessmaps pages 1-3), consistent with the user's observation that Hausner ratio and d50 do not correlate with auger mass per revolution. The angle of repose, which did correlate with the user's dosing data (Spearman −0.84 at 45° tilt), is used in DEM calibration as a standard bulk-flow target (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 1-2, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5) and is one of the most accessible single descriptors of interparticle friction, though it conflates friction and cohesion effects (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5).

---

### 5. Forward–Inverse Model Consistency and Bayesian Optimization for New Materials

**Three architectures for consistency.** The user asks how a model predicting powder properties from dosing data (inverse) and a model predicting dosing from properties (forward) can be kept consistent. The literature suggests three approaches in order of increasing rigor:

(a) **Two separate regressions** is the simplest and most common approach in practice—one PLS or RF model maps properties to feed factor, another maps dosing behavior to a flowability class. This is how most pharmaceutical studies operate (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 18-22, diaz2023machinelearningapproaches pages 4-5). The drawback is that the two models can be mutually inconsistent: a material classified as "cohesive" by the inverse model may be predicted to have acceptable feed factor by the forward model.

(b) **Bayesian inversion of a forward model** is the natural architecture for the user's DEM twin. The forward model (DEM or a trained surrogate) maps particle-level properties (friction, cohesion, rolling friction) to observable dosing fingerprints (mass per revolution, tap-freed mass, afterflow). Bayesian inference—using MCMC, sequential Monte Carlo, or simulation-based inference—then inverts the forward model to obtain a posterior distribution over particle properties given observed data. El Kassem et al. (2021) accomplished this via contour-plot intersection from a regression surrogate (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13). Kim et al. (2026) demonstrated Bridged SBI for the same task, using neural posterior estimation with a residual correction bridge between low- and high-fidelity DEM (kim2026bridgedsbicorrecting pages 1-2, kim2026bridgedsbicorrecting pages 2-3). Fransen et al. (2025) reviewed Bayesian inference for granular-material simulations, formulating the state–parameter model with process and measurement uncertainties and noting that surrogate models (Gaussian processes, neural networks) are needed to make posterior sampling tractable (fransen2026towardsscientificmachine pages 14-16). This architecture ensures automatic consistency: every property value that the inverse model returns is also the input that the forward model would use to predict the observed behavior.

(c) **A joint latent-variable model** would posit that each powder has a low-dimensional latent representation (e.g., a "flow phenotype") from which both the dosing fingerprint and the standard-test properties are generated. PCA or PLS already implicitly provide such a latent space when applied jointly to dosing and property data. No published study was found that implements a fully Bayesian joint latent-variable model specifically for powder dosing, though the pharmaceutical material-library framework of Wang et al. (2019) uses PCA to place materials in a latent space that simultaneously represents flow behavior, feeder performance, and material similarity (wang2019developmentandapplications pages 19-23, wang2019developmentandapplications pages 10-15).

**Bayesian optimization for feeding/dosing of new materials.** The most advanced published implementation is the Digital Formulator and self-driving Tableting DataFactory of Abbas et al. (2025, 2026). The Digital Formulator uses a forward model—ensembles of 20 deep neural networks predicting tablet porosity and tensile strength from raw-material attributes, formulation composition, and compression pressure—validated by leave-API-out testing. It optimizes formulation to maximize flowability (ffc) while constraining tablet quality, using NSGA-II for in-silico search. The Tableting DataFactory then applies physics-informed Bayesian optimization to refine process parameters, typically converging in fewer than six iterations (abbas2025acceleratedmedicinesdevelopment pages 23-26, abbas2025acceleratedmedicinesdevelopment pages 4-8, abbas2025acceleratedmedicinesdevelopment pages 20-23, abbas2025acceleratedmedicinesdevelopment pages 1-4). The powder-dosing system uses a volumetric dispenser whose chamber volume, vacuum duration, and air pressure are adjusted based on density and particle properties, with real-time weighing to reject doses outside ±5% of target (abbas2026accelerateddrugdevelopment pages 4-4, abbas2026accelerateddrugdevelopment pages 11-12). This platform demonstrates the principle of using a forward model to initialize process settings for a new material and then refining them via closed-loop Bayesian optimization—directly applicable to the user's auger doser.

For the user's system specifically, the recommended workflow would be: (1) measure a compact property set (angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, PSD by sieving or laser diffraction, and moisture) on each of the 13+ powders; (2) build a forward PLS or Gaussian-process model mapping these properties to the dosing fingerprint; (3) for Bayesian inversion, train a surrogate on the existing DEM twin (20–50 parameter combinations, each requiring 26–30 CPU-minutes), then use simulation-based inference or MCMC to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling-friction parameters given the observed fingerprint; (4) validate inferred values against measured properties where available; and (5) for a new powder, use the forward model's prediction as the initial setting and prior for Bayesian optimization of auger speed and tilt, closing the loop with the balance feedback already implemented. Multi-fidelity inference via Bridged SBI (kim2026bridgedsbicorrecting pages 1-2) could reduce the DEM budget by using coarse-grained simulations for initial exploration and full-resolution runs only for refinement.

**Forward models (properties → feeder performance).** The most systematic forward-model program is from the Ghent/FDA collaborative group. Bostijn et al. Benedetti built a multivariate weighted PLS (MwPLS) model for a single material across 34 batches, predicting feed-factor profiles from hopper weight and flow-rate setpoint with calibration R² = 0.91 and external-validation R² averaging 0.87 (pqac-00000001). Rezaeizadeh (2026) compared PLS, random forest, Gaussian-process regression, and SVR for feed-factor-profile prediction, finding all models achieved MAPE < 5%, with PLS including material properties yielding RMSECV of 0.118 g versus 0.122 g for RF without material properties—a marginal improvement (pqac-00000002).

**Inverse models (process signals → powder properties).** Diaz et al. (2023) used 112 pharmaceutical systems (30 APIs, 43 excipients, 40 blends) characterized by dynamic image analysis (D10, D50, D90, aspect ratio, sphericity) and bulk density to classify powders into flow-function-coefficient (FFc) classes (cohesive, easy-flowing, free-flowing). Among six classifiers (MLP, RF, SVM, kNN, naïve Bayes, AdaBoost), MLP achieved the highest single-step ROC-AUC of 0.823 under 10-fold cross-validation, though the middle "easy-flowing" class was classified below 45% correct (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031). In the companion thesis, a random-forest model on 103 formulations predicted continuous FFc with MAPE = 0.173 and wall-friction angle with MAE = 1.83°, using SHAP to reveal that API D10, D50, and aspect ratio D10 were the most predictive features (pqac-00000024). Owasit et al. (2025) assembled 410 blends from 9 APIs and 18 excipients, classifying flow regimes (2–5 classes defined by FFc thresholds) with RF, XGBoost, SVM, logistic regression, kNN, and MLP. RF performed best, reaching approximately 85% accuracy for two-class individual components, 94.67% for uncoated blends, and 81.36% on an entirely unseen API (IBU25) for two classes, though accuracy declined to 45.76% for five classes (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). SHAP analysis identified dry-coating parameters as the most influential features, followed by particle size and morphology (pqac-00000028).

---

### 2. Model Classes and Practices for Datasets of 10–40 Materials

The following table compares model families evaluated on small powder datasets.

| Model class | Suitability for 10–40 materials | Main advantages | Main limitations / safeguards | Relevant evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS / OPLS | **Very suitable; recommended baseline.** Particularly useful when descriptors outnumber materials or are strongly correlated. | Latent variables provide implicit regularization; handles collinear flow, density and PSD descriptors; loadings/VIP scores aid interpretation; supports multi-response models. | Primarily linear; latent-component count must be selected inside cross-validation; interactions or transforms should be prespecified sparingly. In a 45-material study, reliability largely stabilized at about **20 representative materials**; stratified selection helped below 15. | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048) |
| Ridge / elastic net / lasso | **Suitable**, especially as a transparent benchmark with engineered physics features. | Explicit L2/L1 regularization controls variance; ridge is stable with correlated predictors; lasso can produce a compact descriptor panel; elastic net combines both benefits. | Linear unless interactions or splines are added; lasso may select one arbitrary member of a correlated group; scaling and nested selection of the penalty parameter are essential. | Ridge-regularized response surfaces were used successfully in a 34-point DEM-surrogate study (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000066). |
| Gaussian-process regression | **Excellent for very small, low-dimensional datasets** when calibrated uncertainty is important. | Posterior mean and variance support Bayesian calibration, active learning and constrained Bayesian optimization; kernels encode smoothness, monotonic trends and physics-informed distances. | Kernel and prior choices are decisive; sensitive to input scaling and non-smooth regime changes such as no-flow/flow transitions. With 34 DEM points, GPR achieved **R² = 0.976 ± 0.023** for belt mass flow but only **0.384** for nonlinear silo discharge. | (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000066) |
| Random forest | **Reasonable from roughly 30 independent observations**, or more when responses are highly variable. | Captures nonlinearities and interactions with little preprocessing; robust to monotone transforms; SHAP and permutation importance aid interpretation; useful for mixed continuous/categorical descriptors. | Piecewise-constant predictions extrapolate poorly; uncertainty is not inherently Bayesian; unstable feature importance under correlated predictors; can overfit tiny material-level datasets despite many within-material repeats. RF reached about **85%** two-class accuracy for constituent powders and **81.36%** on an unseen API. | (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000063) |
| Gradient boosting—XGBoost / CatBoost | **Potentially useful but usually more data-hungry than regularized linear models**; treat as a challenger rather than the primary model at 10–20 materials. | Strong nonlinear regression/classification; captures threshold effects and interactions; CatBoost handles categorical factors; SHAP interpretation is available. | Many hyperparameters create high selection variance; needs nested grouped validation, shallow trees and conservative regularization. GBM gave **R² = 0.883** for 34-point silo discharge, below ANN and RF; CatBoost has been used for FFc regression. | (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000063) |
| Neural networks—MLP / DNN | **Generally high risk below 40–50 independent materials** unless the architecture is tiny, strongly regularized or pretrained on simulation/library data. | Flexible multi-output mapping; can fuse distributions, images and scalar properties; ensembles provide empirical uncertainty; suitable for large simulation-generated datasets. | Parameter count can dwarf material count; repeated runs from the same material do not solve this; requires early stopping, weight decay, ensembling and material-grouped validation. MLP achieved **ROC-AUC = 0.823** on 112 powder systems; the Digital Formulator used 20-member DNN ensembles and leave-API-out testing. | (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036) |
| Response-surface methodology | **Excellent for designed simulation/experimental campaigns of about 20–34 points with few factors.** | Interpretable linear, quadratic and interaction terms; efficient for calibration and optimization; coefficients and derivatives expose physical trends. | Scales poorly with dimension; fixed polynomials miss discontinuities, hysteresis and complex local structure; design space must be bounded. With 34 DEM points, RSM achieved **R² = 0.999 ± 0.001** for belt discharge angle; a 20-run auger DEM design produced mean deviation **0.87%**. | (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000066) |
| Bayesian latent-variable / hierarchical multi-output models | **Conceptually best for the proposed 13–40-material campaign**, although implementation is more demanding and direct feeder precedents are limited. | Represents latent powder state, repeated-run variation, label uncertainty and correlated outputs jointly; incorporates literature values as uncertain priors; enables coherent forward prediction and Bayesian inversion; posterior uncertainty can drive active learning or BO. | Requires explicit identifiability constraints and careful priors; computation and diagnostics are more involved; posterior multimodality is likely when several DEM parameters produce similar fingerprints. Surrogates or multi-fidelity SBI may be needed for expensive DEM. | Bayesian DEM calibration supports parameter distributions and correlations; Bridged SBI reduced posterior KL divergence by up to **75%** versus naïve multi-fidelity inference under a small high-fidelity budget (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058). |


*Table: Comparison of model families for datasets containing roughly 10–40 independent powders, emphasizing data efficiency, uncertainty, nonlinear capability, and safeguards against material-level leakage.*

**PLS as the recommended baseline.** For pharmaceutical material-library modeling, Cao et al. (2024) systematically investigated PLS sample-size requirements using a 45-material library with 27 physical-property descriptors predicting tablet tensile strength. Performance (minimum R² and RMSE) stabilized and remained nearly unchanged as sample size increased from 20 to 45 materials, indicating that approximately 20 diverse materials suffice for dependable PLS prediction (pqac-00000047). Below 15 materials, hierarchical sampling based on a tabletability classification index d was more reliable than random sampling, reducing the incidence of low-quality few-shot models (pqac-00000046). For the user's 13-material set, PLS is therefore feasible but near the lower limit; expanding to 20–25 materials with deliberately diverse flow behavior would improve stability.

**Handling repeated measurements, censored data, and noisy labels.** Multiple measurements per material (e.g., six single-revolution mass values at each tilt angle) should be treated as repeated measures within a material-level statistical unit, not as independent observations. Material should be the blocking factor in cross-validation (leave-one-material-out or grouped k-fold), as demonstrated by Wang/Li's leave-one-material-out scheme (pqac-00000000) and Limhengha et al.'s replicate-aware grouped five-fold cross-validation, which assigns all replicates of a design point to the same fold to prevent leakage (pqac-00000060). Censored responses (five powders that barely convey, yielding near-zero mass per revolution) can be handled by Tobit-style censored regression within PLS or by treating the threshold between "no flow" and "flow" as a binary classification layer preceding a continuous regression for flowing materials (a two-step scheme analogous to Diaz et al.'s two-step FFc classifier) (pqac-00000025). Literature-derived property values with wide reported ranges (e.g., angle of repose 6–16°) introduce label noise that can be modeled by Bayesian measurement-error or errors-in-variables extensions, or by treating literature values as informative priors and updating them as measured values become available (pqac-00000058).

**Validation.** Leave-one-material-out cross-validation is the gold standard for material-level generalization with 10–20 materials (pqac-00000000). With more materials, nested cross-validation (inner loop for hyperparameter tuning, outer for performance estimation) is preferred. Prospective tests on genuinely new materials provide the strongest evidence: Bostijn et al. validated on two held-out powders (pqac-00000004), and Owasit et al. tested on an entirely unseen API (pqac-00000027).

---

### 3. Combining Physics-Based and Data-Driven Models

Several strategies for integrating DEM, Beverloo, Jenike, or screw-conveyor models with data-driven approaches have been demonstrated.

**DEM-generated training data.** Desai and Higgs (2019) calibrated a polydispersed DEM model of Ti-6Al-4V powder spreading against rheometer data, then ran approximately 50 virtual spreading simulations varying spreader translation and rotation speeds. The DEM outputs (retained mass, throughput, roughness, porosity) served as noise-free training data for a back-propagation neural network with one hidden layer of 200 sigmoid neurons. The trained surrogate achieved ≥96% accuracy and was used to generate spreading process maps, enabling rapid exploration that would be prohibitively expensive with DEM alone (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042). This approach maps directly onto the user's situation: each auger revolution costs 26–30 CPU-minutes in DEM, so a design of 20–50 DEM simulations spanning friction coefficients and speed could train a surrogate that runs in milliseconds.

**DEM-based calibration with DoE and regression.** El Kassem et al. (2021) used a vertical auger doser as the calibration device, extracting angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate as three experimentally measurable bulk responses. A D-optimal design of experiments varying four DEM input factors (auger speed, particle–particle static and rolling friction, particle–wall static friction) was simulated in LIGGGHTS with Hertz–Mindlin contact and EPSD2 rolling resistance. Multivariate regression analysis built prediction models from only 20 DEM simulations. Superimposing contour plots of the three predicted responses dramatically reduced admissible parameter combinations, yielding an optimized set with maximum deviation of 2.86% for dosing time and mean deviation of 0.87% across 12 bulk responses (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). This workflow directly parallels the user's DEM twin and shows that multiple bulk responses (their dosing fingerprint) can be used jointly to constrain DEM parameters.

**Multi-fidelity and transfer learning.** Kim et al. (2026) introduced Bridged Simulation-Based Inference (Bridged SBI) for cost-efficient Bayesian calibration of particle-based simulators. The method uses inexpensive low-fidelity DEM simulations (coarser particles, fewer particles) to identify a coarse posterior region, then trains a residual correction or transport bridge using a small number of high-fidelity simulations. In real-to-sim experiments calibrating friction and restitution of granular soil from depth images, Bridged SBI achieved KL divergence of 2.79 ± 0.77 at a total budget of N = 7 high-fidelity evaluations, compared with 11.19 ± 6.80 for naïve multi-fidelity SBI and 6.53 ± 3.62 for high-fidelity-only SBI—a 75% and 67% reduction respectively (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055). This approach is directly applicable to the user's scenario: a coarse-grained DEM at 6× particle diameter (as used by Kassem et al.) could serve as the low-fidelity simulator, while the current full-resolution model provides the high-fidelity simulator, with a small number of full-resolution runs used to debias the coarse posterior.

**Surrogate model selection for DEM outputs.** Limhengha and Sudsawat (2026) compared five surrogate families—RSM, ANN, RF, GBM, and GPR—on 34 DEM design points for silo discharge and belt-conveyor responses. They found that the best algorithm is response-specific: ANN achieved R² = 0.964 for silo discharge mass flow rate, while GPR attained R² = 0.976 for belt mass-flow but only 0.384 for silo discharge, and RSM reached R² = 0.999 for belt discharge angle (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063). SHAP analysis confirmed physical expectations (outlet width dominated silo flow with 78.6% importance) and the proposed SHAP Asymmetry Ratio offered a diagnostic for algorithm pre-selection (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000064).

**Physics-informed features.** While granular Bond number (ratio of cohesive to gravitational force) and orifice-to-particle size ratio are well-established dimensionless groups in the powder-flow literature (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015), and Girnth et al. (2024) specifically advocated formula-based dimensionless DEM parameterization for additive manufacturing, the retrieved studies did not demonstrate a completed workflow using these features as explicit ML inputs for feeder prediction. Incorporating such physics-informed features into the user's PLS or GP models—for example, using the ratio of auger outlet diameter to D50 rather than each separately—would reduce dimensionality and improve out-of-domain extrapolation.

---

### 4. Dataset Size Requirements and Most Predictive Descriptors

**How many materials are needed.** For PLS models, Cao et al. (2024) found that 20 materials produced stable performance equivalent to 45 materials, and that hierarchical sampling gave more reliable few-shot models when libraries contained fewer than 15 materials (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047). For ML classifiers, Owasit et al. (2025) used 89 single-component measurements from 27 distinct materials to train RF classifiers achieving 85% accuracy (pqac-00000028). Bostijn et al. (2019) built useful PLS models from 13 calibration materials plus 2 external (pqac-00000004). Collectively, these suggest that 15–20 diverse materials provide a practical lower bound for regression models, while 10–13 may suffice for coarser classification or ranking tasks. The user's 13 powders, spanning more than three decades of mass per revolution, provide substantial diversity but are near the minimum; adding 7–12 materials (metal AM powders, sieved fractions, humidity-conditioned salt) as planned would substantially improve reliability.

**Most predictive descriptors for small feeders.** Across the literature, conditioned bulk density (cBD) emerges as the single strongest correlate of feed factor and mass flow rate in screw feeders (pqac-00000010). Beyond this, the most informative descriptor sets include: (i) compressibility at a defined stress, which reflects interparticle cohesion and predicts feed-factor decay at changing hopper levels (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015); (ii) flow-function coefficient (ffc) from shear-cell testing, the standard cohesion/flowability classifier (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000024); (iii) particle-size distribution measures D10, D50, and D90, with D10 and D50 identified as the most important SHAP features for FFc prediction (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030); (iv) particle shape (aspect ratio and sphericity), which affects mechanical interlocking and flow through small orifices (pqac-00000029); (v) permeability, which governs air-entrainment and de-aeration behavior during feeding (pqac-00000012); (vi) dynamic flow energy (BFE, specific energy, stability index), which reflects flow behavior under active agitation such as screw rotation (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008); and (vii) charge density, which was included in the Bostijn et al. descriptor set (pqac-00000004). Wall friction angle is important for hopper and die-filling contexts (pqac-00000024) but was not identified as a dominant feed-factor predictor. Moisture was recognized as influential through capillary forces and electrostatic effects (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015), though its role was not isolated in the retrieved feeder-specific models.

Wang et al. (2019) demonstrated that for routine flow characterization, a reduced set of four tests—compressibility, permeability, and shear-cell measurements at 3 and 9 kPa—captured flow-classification structure equivalent to the full test battery, consuming approximately 50 g and three instrument-hours per material (pqac-00000011). This represents a practical minimum measurement set for the user's planned characterization.

**Relevance to additive manufacturing spreadability.** Hall flow time does not correlate with spread-layer density in AM (pqac-00000043), consistent with the user's observation that Hausner ratio and d50 do not correlate with auger mass per revolution. The angle of repose, which did correlate with the user's dosing data (Spearman −0.84 at 45° tilt), is used in DEM calibration as a standard bulk-flow target (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) and is one of the most accessible single descriptors of interparticle friction, though it conflates friction and cohesion effects (pqac-00000019).

---

### 5. Forward–Inverse Model Consistency and Bayesian Optimization for New Materials

**Three architectures for consistency.** The user asks how a model predicting powder properties from dosing data (inverse) and a model predicting dosing from properties (forward) can be kept consistent. The literature suggests three approaches in order of increasing rigor:

(a) **Two separate regressions** is the simplest and most common approach in practice—one PLS or RF model maps properties to feed factor, another maps dosing behavior to a flowability class. This is how most pharmaceutical studies operate (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000029). The drawback is that the two models can be mutually inconsistent: a material classified as "cohesive" by the inverse model may be predicted to have acceptable feed factor by the forward model.

(b) **Bayesian inversion of a forward model** is the natural architecture for the user's DEM twin. The forward model (DEM or a trained surrogate) maps particle-level properties (friction, cohesion, rolling friction) to observable dosing fingerprints (mass per revolution, tap-freed mass, afterflow). Bayesian inference—using MCMC, sequential Monte Carlo, or simulation-based inference—then inverts the forward model to obtain a posterior distribution over particle properties given observed data. El Kassem et al. (2021) accomplished this via contour-plot intersection from a regression surrogate (pqac-00000020). Kim et al. (2026) demonstrated Bridged SBI for the same task, using neural posterior estimation with a residual correction bridge between low- and high-fidelity DEM (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000054). Fransen et al. (2025) reviewed Bayesian inference for granular-material simulations, formulating the state–parameter model with process and measurement uncertainties and noting that surrogate models (Gaussian processes, neural networks) are needed to make posterior sampling tractable (pqac-00000058). This architecture ensures automatic consistency: every property value that the inverse model returns is also the input that the forward model would use to predict the observed behavior.

(c) **A joint latent-variable model** would posit that each powder has a low-dimensional latent representation (e.g., a "flow phenotype") from which both the dosing fingerprint and the standard-test properties are generated. PCA or PLS already implicitly provide such a latent space when applied jointly to dosing and property data. No published study was found that implements a fully Bayesian joint latent-variable model specifically for powder dosing, though the pharmaceutical material-library framework of Wang et al. (2019) uses PCA to place materials in a latent space that simultaneously represents flow behavior, feeder performance, and material similarity (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014).

**Bayesian optimization for feeding/dosing of new materials.** The most advanced published implementation is the Digital Formulator and self-driving Tableting DataFactory of Abbas et al. (2025, 2026). The Digital Formulator uses a forward model—ensembles of 20 deep neural networks predicting tablet porosity and tensile strength from raw-material attributes, formulation composition, and compression pressure—validated by leave-API-out testing. It optimizes formulation to maximize flowability (ffc) while constraining tablet quality, using NSGA-II for in-silico search. The Tableting DataFactory then applies physics-informed Bayesian optimization to refine process parameters, typically converging in fewer than six iterations (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038). The powder-dosing system uses a volumetric dispenser whose chamber volume, vacuum duration, and air pressure are adjusted based on density and particle properties, with real-time weighing to reject doses outside ±5% of target (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). This platform demonstrates the principle of using a forward model to initialize process settings for a new material and then refining them via closed-loop Bayesian optimization—directly applicable to the user's auger doser.

For the user's system specifically, the recommended workflow would be: (1) measure a compact property set (angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, PSD by sieving or laser diffraction, and moisture) on each of the 13+ powders; (2) build a forward PLS or Gaussian-process model mapping these properties to the dosing fingerprint; (3) for Bayesian inversion, train a surrogate on the existing DEM twin (20–50 parameter combinations, each requiring 26–30 CPU-minutes), then use simulation-based inference or MCMC to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling-friction parameters given the observed fingerprint; (4) validate inferred values against measured properties where available; and (5) for a new powder, use the forward model's prediction as the initial setting and prior for Bayesian optimization of auger speed and tilt, closing the loop with the balance feedback already implemented. Multi-fidelity inference via Bridged SBI (pqac-00000051) could reduce the DEM budget by using coarse-grained simulations for initial exploration and full-resolution runs only for refinement.

contexts.context: Seven powder materials were tested. The predictor descriptors consisted of 30 material flow properties plus one process variable: drive command, defined as the percentage of maximum screw speed required to maintain the common 8 kg/h feed rate. Feeder/doser refill performance was represented by three responses: maximum deviation (the difference between the maximum refill feed rate and the target setpoint), deviation time (the duration associated with the out-of-specification transition between volumetric and gravimetric operation), and percentage total deviation (%Total), the excess mass relative to the target feeding mass. The main predictive model was partial least squares regression (PLSR), with material properties and drive command as X variables and each of the three quantified deviations as separate Y responses. PCA followed by weighted Euclidean similarity scoring (PCA-SS) was also used for material similarity and qualitative performance prediction; it identified fine zeolite as most similar to Material A, whose refill behavior was experimentally similar. Validation used a leave-one-material-out procedure: each of the six materials was treated in turn as the held-out ‘Material A,’ while the remaining six were used for calibration. The excerpt reports that measured and PLSR-predicted deviations differed only minorly, indicating successful prediction, but it does not provide numerical accuracy metrics such as R², RMSE, or percentage error.

contexts.context: The study tested feeder data for one material only. No material characterization properties or descriptors were used as model inputs. The available feeder variables were weight, screw speed, mass flowrate, and feed factor; the modelling strategy used mass-flowrate setpoint as the equipment/setup input and weight as the only known dynamic predictor, while predicting the feed-factor profile. Screw speed and mass flowrate profiles were not included as predictors because they would be unknown when making a new prediction. A multivariate weighted partial least-squares model (MwPLS) was built. Of 34 realized batches, 30 were used for calibration and four batches (#3, #12, #19, and #27), spanning the tested flowrates, were randomly reserved as an external validation set. The two-component model explained 96.2% of the X-block variance and 39.7% of the Y-block variance. Feed-factor fitting achieved an average calibration R² of 0.91.
