artifacts.artifact-01:
| Model class | Suitability for 10–40 materials | Main advantages | Main limitations / safeguards | Relevant evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS / OPLS | **Very suitable; recommended baseline.** Particularly useful when descriptors outnumber materials or are strongly correlated. | Latent variables provide implicit regularization; handles collinear flow, density and PSD descriptors; loadings/VIP scores aid interpretation; supports multi-response models. | Primarily linear; latent-component count must be selected inside cross-validation; interactions or transforms should be prespecified sparingly. In a 45-material study, reliability largely stabilized at about **20 representative materials**; stratified selection helped below 15. | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048) |
| Ridge / elastic net / lasso | **Suitable**, especially as a transparent benchmark with engineered physics features. | Explicit L2/L1 regularization controls variance; ridge is stable with correlated predictors; lasso can produce a compact descriptor panel; elastic net combines both benefits. | Linear unless interactions or splines are added; lasso may select one arbitrary member of a correlated group; scaling and nested selection of the penalty parameter are essential. | Ridge-regularized response surfaces were used successfully in a 34-point DEM-surrogate study (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000066). |
| Gaussian-process regression | **Excellent for very small, low-dimensional datasets** when calibrated uncertainty is important. | Posterior mean and variance support Bayesian calibration, active learning and constrained Bayesian optimization; kernels encode smoothness, monotonic trends and physics-informed distances. | Kernel and prior choices are decisive; sensitive to input scaling and non-smooth regime changes such as no-flow/flow transitions. With 34 DEM points, GPR achieved **R² = 0.976 ± 0.023** for belt mass flow but only **0.384** for nonlinear silo discharge. | (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000066) |
| Random forest | **Reasonable from roughly 30 independent observations**, or more when responses are highly variable. | Captures nonlinearities and interactions with little preprocessing; robust to monotone transforms; SHAP and permutation importance aid interpretation; useful for mixed continuous/categorical descriptors. | Piecewise-constant predictions extrapolate poorly; uncertainty is not inherently Bayesian; unstable feature importance under correlated predictors; can overfit tiny material-level datasets despite many within-material repeats. RF reached about **85%** two-class accuracy for constituent powders and **81.36%** on an unseen API. | (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000063) |
| Gradient boosting—XGBoost / CatBoost | **Potentially useful but usually more data-hungry than regularized linear models**; treat as a challenger rather than the primary model at 10–20 materials. | Strong nonlinear regression/classification; captures threshold effects and interactions; CatBoost handles categorical factors; SHAP interpretation is available. | Many hyperparameters create high selection variance; needs nested grouped validation, shallow trees and conservative regularization. GBM gave **R² = 0.883** for 34-point silo discharge, below ANN and RF; CatBoost has been used for FFc regression. | (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000063) |
| Neural networks—MLP / DNN | **Generally high risk below 40–50 independent materials** unless the architecture is tiny, strongly regularized or pretrained on simulation/library data. | Flexible multi-output mapping; can fuse distributions, images and scalar properties; ensembles provide empirical uncertainty; suitable for large simulation-generated datasets. | Parameter count can dwarf material count; repeated runs from the same material do not solve this; requires early stopping, weight decay, ensembling and material-grouped validation. MLP achieved **ROC-AUC = 0.823** on 112 powder systems; the Digital Formulator used 20-member DNN ensembles and leave-API-out testing. | (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036) |
| Response-surface methodology | **Excellent for designed simulation/experimental campaigns of about 20–34 points with few factors.** | Interpretable linear, quadratic and interaction terms; efficient for calibration and optimization; coefficients and derivatives expose physical trends. | Scales poorly with dimension; fixed polynomials miss discontinuities, hysteresis and complex local structure; design space must be bounded. With 34 DEM points, RSM achieved **R² = 0.999 ± 0.001** for belt discharge angle; a 20-run auger DEM design produced mean deviation **0.87%**. | (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000066) |
| Bayesian latent-variable / hierarchical multi-output models | **Conceptually best for the proposed 13–40-material campaign**, although implementation is more demanding and direct feeder precedents are limited. | Represents latent powder state, repeated-run variation, label uncertainty and correlated outputs jointly; incorporates literature values as uncertain priors; enables coherent forward prediction and Bayesian inversion; posterior uncertainty can drive active learning or BO. | Requires explicit identifiability constraints and careful priors; computation and diagnostics are more involved; posterior multimodality is likely when several DEM parameters produce similar fingerprints. Surrogates or multi-fidelity SBI may be needed for expensive DEM. | Bayesian DEM calibration supports parameter distributions and correlations; Bridged SBI reduced posterior KL divergence by up to **75%** versus naïve multi-fidelity inference under a small high-fidelity budget (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058). |


*Table: Comparison of model families for datasets containing roughly 10–40 independent powders, emphasizing data efficiency, uncertainty, nonlinear capability, and safeguards against material-level leakage.*

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Our data so far: 13 powders (NaCl, Si 75-150 um and Si <44 um, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, Na2SO4, BaCl2 dihydrate, calcium lactate, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, sodium alginate, white and brown rice flour, fumed silica), each run once through a fixed protocol on a cone-exit auger: mass per revolution at 0, 22.5 and 45 degree tube tilt (30 rpm, six single revolutions each), a speed exponent from 15 to 90 rpm, mass released per solenoid tap, mass that flows during a 15 s static hold, and closed-loop doses of 50, 200 and 1000 mg (error, time, pass rate). Mass per revolution spans more than three decades and five powders barely convey. The property values we have are handbook or supplier values for each material class (angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, Hausner ratio, d50, true density, equilibrium moisture), not measurements on our lots, and their published ranges are wide (angle of repose ranges 6-16 degrees). Literature angle of repose correlates with log mass per revolution at 45 degrees (Spearman -0.84); d50 and Hausner ratio do not. We plan to measure angle of repose, PSD, bulk and tapped density and moisture on the same jars, to add powders (metal AM powders, sieved size fractions, humidity-conditioned salt), and we have the DEM twin described above. Questions: (1) Which published studies built statistical or machine-learning models that predict feeder or doser performance (feed factor, mass flow rate, flow variability, feeding capacity, refill behaviour, dosing accuracy) from raw-material properties, for example material property libraries with PCA or PLS for loss-in-weight, screw and micro-feeders, and which studies predicted powder properties (flowability class, ffc, Hausner ratio, cohesion, particle size, moisture) from process or flow signals (feeder, rotating drum or avalanche tester, vibrating capillary, hopper or funnel discharge)? For each, give the number of materials, the descriptors and responses, the model, the validation scheme and the accuracy reached. (2) For datasets of 10-40 materials, which model classes and practices work best (PLS, ridge or lasso, Gaussian processes, random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks, Bayesian latent-variable or multi-output models, monotone or physics-constrained models)? How should repeated measurements per material, censored responses (no flow), and noisy or literature-derived property labels be handled, and how should models be validated (leave-one-material-out, nested cross-validation, prospective tests on new materials)? (3) How have physics-based models (DEM, Beverloo, Jenike or screw-conveyor models) been combined with data-driven models in this setting: simulation-generated training data, physics-informed features such as granular Bond number or orifice-to-particle size ratio, residual or discrepancy learning, multi-fidelity or transfer learning, and with what measured gains? (4) How many materials and which measurements are typically needed to reach useful accuracy, and which descriptors have proven most predictive of flow in small feeders (cohesion or ffc, wall friction, bulk density, PSD width, particle shape, moisture, electrostatics)? (5) How can a model that predicts properties from dosing data and a model that predicts dosing from properties be kept consistent (one joint latent-variable model, Bayesian inversion of a forward model, or two separate regressions), and have such models been used to choose initial settings, priors or task descriptors for Bayesian optimization of feeding or dosing for a new material?
